title: Governor. ICMB. Europe in the new geopolitical landscape
summary: José Luis Escrivá’s Geneva lecture argues that several advantages on which European firms previously relied have become less dependable at the same time. Security, access to export markets, imported energy and foreign technology were all available within an international order favourable to Europe. Demographic change now puts pressure on labour supply while geopolitical rivalry, the energy transition and AI demand new investment. Escrivá’s response is to connect Europe’s existing savings, skills, science and single market more effectively. The examples in the lecture describe legal and financial infrastructure that could enable that investment, without putting a number on the aggregate return.

The population chart on slide 4 puts the scale of the labour problem in perspective. It shows Europe potentially losing approximately one in five working-age people by 2050 under restrictive migration assumptions. It covers people aged 20–64, so the change is in the size of the population available for work, not a forecast of the number employed. Later slides identify a practical lever: the EU Blue Card offers highly skilled non-EU workers a common route with mobility within the Union after twelve months. An annual average of 83,000 cards was issued in 2022–24, about three quarters in Germany. Other countries still rely heavily on national permits. A common instrument can therefore coexist with very different national patterns of use.

Energy and technology present a related tension. Net imports supplied 57% of EU energy needs, while the supply of several equipment categories for the transition was highly concentrated in China. The lecture reports that China supplied 99% of imported solar panels and 98% of imported rare-earth magnets. These shares refer to imports, not all panels or magnets used in Europe. Electrification, measured as electricity’s share of final consumption, was around 24% in the EU versus 34% in China in the latest comparison on slide 7. Industrial investment in electrification can change fossil-fuel exposure while introducing dependencies in equipment and materials. Slide 8 also shows a wide gap between US and European AI investment. Its European private-investment series includes only Germany, France and Sweden, and the public-investment comparison uses different periods across jurisdictions.

For firms seeking scale, Escrivá supports a proposed optional European company form alongside the 27 national regimes. The proposal envisages rapid online incorporation, limited registration expense and a common employee stock-option arrangement. He would go further on insolvency for start-ups, enforcement of collateral and a single digital registry, and extend integration into tax and labour matters (slide 11). Initial incorporation and subsequent financing are separate hurdles. Common registration matters less to a lender if the timing and enforceability of recoveries continue to depend on local procedures.

Escrivá cites Nordic equity markets as evidence that different outcomes are possible under the same broad EU framework. At end-2025 Denmark, Sweden and Finland together had 55.8 listed companies per million people, compared with 9.5 in the rest of the EU. He points to proportionate rules, tax incentives, funded pensions and household participation. The comparison describes an institutional package and does not isolate the contribution of any one policy. His final example is the Eurosystem’s payments strategy: Pontes would connect private distributed-ledger platforms to settlement in wholesale central-bank money, with Appia providing a longer-term architecture. Across these examples, the investment case depends on whether European scale improves firms’ ability to finance growth and retain talent. None of the illustrations amounts to a near-term monetary-policy commitment.

questions.question: Where would the proposed common company form change the cost of financing?
questions.detail: Fast registration is measurable, but the lecture also identifies collateral enforcement and insolvency as unfinished work. Compare time to incorporation with time to recover pledged assets and the cost of raising the next round in different jurisdictions. Company registers, insolvency statistics and financing surveys could distinguish marginal administrative savings from a real improvement in firms’ financing terms.

questions.question: Could the Nordic equity-market comparison survive adjustment for company size and listing rules?
questions.detail: The listings-per-capita gap is large, yet the lecture attributes it to several institutions acting together. Compare new issues, delistings, pension allocations, secondary liquidity and the size distribution of listings using exchange and pension-supervisor reports. That would help determine whether deeper markets generate investable liquidity and growth finance or mainly a larger count of small listings.

questions.question: Which energy investments would reduce exposure to concentrated suppliers?
questions.detail: Net energy import dependence and the import shares for transition equipment measure different risks. Compare domestic production, supplier concentration, substitution times, grid access and installed equipment for specific technologies in energy-system and trade data. The evidence would identify projects that diversify long-run operating costs while revealing which manufacturers face large new dependencies during construction.

limitation: The Governor published a 16-slide presentation. Slide 4’s heading refers to 2026, while its baseline bar is labelled 2025. No accompanying spoken transcript was available from the publication.
